newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris judge searched Libyan secret service offices.
newsitem.headline: Paris judge searched Libyan secret service offices.

text.p: A French judge searched Libyan secret service offices during a visit to Tripoli and found timers and detonators believed similar to those used to destroy a French airliner over the Sahara, representatives of the victims' families said on Wednesday.

Sources close to the investigation have said that Jean-Louis Bruguiere, France's top anti-terrorism judge, plans to recommend soon that four Libyans be tried in their absence for the mid-air bombing which killed all 170 people aboard a UTA airlines DC-10 on September 19, 1989.
Three of the suspects are intelligence officials, including the brother-in-law of Colonel Muammar Gaddafi, the sources said.

The UTA bombing is linked with the 1988 destruction of a Pan Am flight over Lockerbie, Scotland, by a U.N. resolution which imposed sanctions on Libya in an effort to speed investigations and bring suspects to trial in the West.
Bruguiere questioned some 40 people during 12 days in Libya in July and brought back a U.S.-made Samsonite suitcase he believes is identical to that packed with pentrite and used in the bombing.

"Apart from the suitcase, which had the same serial number and was the same colour as that used in the bombing, Bruguiere obtained other evidence during searches of Libyan secret service offices in Tripoli," Francoise Rudetski, head of the victims' association SOS Attentats told Reuters.
"The judge obtained timers and detonators comparable to those which were reportedly used to set off the explosives in the plane," she said.

Rudetski added that Bruguiere had been unable to question the four suspects he wants to be tried in absentia because under French law he would have had to meet them in his Paris offices and in the presence of their lawyers.
The suspects include Abdallah Senoussi, a brother-in-law of Gaddafi identified as a senior Libyan intelligence official.
The other suspects are Abdallah Elazragh, a diplomat working in Brazzaville at the time, and alleged secret agents Ibrahim Naeli and Musbah Arbas.
Seven years to the day after the crash, Bruguiere will on Thursday brief some 200 civil plaintiffs at the Paris Palais de Justice on his findings, completing his investigation.
He will also take those families who wish to go to see a painstaking reconstruction of the airliner at the military airport of Le Bourget outside Paris.

The destruction of the DC-10, in which citizens of more than a dozen countries were killed, occurred at the height of tension between France and Libya over Chad, where the two countries' armies clashed repeatedly in the 1970s and 1980s.
Investigators have recovered some 80 percent of the doomed plane and have worked out to within a square metre where the bomb went off in the forward cargo loading bay.

The U.N. Security Council imposed economic sanctions on Libya over its refusal to hand over suspects in the DC-10 blast and in the 1988 explosion of Pan Am flight 103 over Lockerbie, Scotland, which killed 270 people.
